articles.title: The Alonetimes review – frenetic, funny and exhilarating music theatre
articles.description: Sohmen Concert Hall, Schwarzman Centre, Oxford Six performers navigate a disjointed world of online slang, loneliness and absurdity in the UK premiere of Jennifer Walshe and Philip Venables’ thrillingly original collaboration As we found our seats, a druidic figure wearing a string of vapes as a necklace sat on stage swathed in white fabric and smoke, emitting close-miked mouth noises amid a rising chorus of percussive hisses and rattles. Then dancing flashlights, reverb and thunderous drum rolls. Later came monologues delivered with quiet, skin-crawling sincerity or pounded out as a kind of manic rap and comically dysfunctional text chats projected on the backcloth. Not to mention the dance breaks. There was an angular, hyper-controlled trio fluent in the language of modern ballet and a hands-on-hips traditional number as faux-folk lyrics scrolled in gothic script and a hefty synthetic beat throbbed below. The first collaboration between Jennifer Walshe and Philip Venables – two of the most distinctive creators in music theatre today – The Alonetimes was never likely to adhere to the conventional playbook of opera. The programme for its UK premiere describes the work as “a fragmented archaeology of personal stories”. Alternatively: there is no single linear plot but instead six performers, who step constantly in and out of unnamed roles, switch between playing instruments and singing, form a taut Greek chorus and stand alone in the spotlights. articles.title: Cyberpunk: Edgerunners Season 2 Is More Punk Rock Than Blockbuster
articles.description: Cyberpunk: Edgerunners Season Two once again sees Studio Trigger handle animation duties, and this time, the anime powerhouse has gotten even wilder with its depiction of Night City and its residents. While the first season was bold in its visual direction, director Kai Ikarashi has pushed it even further, using more abstract shapes and experimental animation techniques to capture the look and feel of a cutting-edge dystopia. What does that lead to? A new season that showrunner Bartosz Sztybor calls a shift from Michael Bay-directed movies to Martin Scorsese-inspired (absolute) cinema. "I think the difference for me is—and I think I once made this reference—visually, the first season was very Michael Bay, while this second season is more like Martin Scorsese," Sztybor said to GameSpot. "He uses shapes and light differently. Even if the backgrounds are the same real places from the game, and Studio Trigger was sometimes using the same assets, the way he recreates them is different. It fits the vibe of the story, which is also very different. It's not this huge emotional thing, but rather something indie, more punkish, and more realistic. For example, the violence in season two feels more striking and real to me personally—more shocking, even if it's not as over-the-top as in season one." Ikarashi and Studio Trigger's visual direction for this new season allows for a range of Cyberpunk topics. From cyber-psychosis (where heavily augmented people violently lose their grip on reality) to an all-powerful AI program sharing space with your mind, the result is a series that doesn't look like a stereotypical anime series. Ikarashi has made a name for himself as a key animator on several anime series that have reflected his abstract tastes, like the critically acclaimed Bocchi the Rock, Mob Psycho 100, and Evangelion: 3.0+1.0 Thrice Upon a Time, so if you're familiar with his work, you'll have an idea of what to expect in the new Edgerunners series. This theme of experimentation also extends to the character Roman, a young cinephile who serves as the point-of-view character in Edgerunners. Always armed with an analogue camera, a large chunk of the show is seen through the low-resolution 4:3 lens of his device. Sztybor added that Roman became a pivotal part of the story after he discovered that both he and Ikarashi were cinephiles. "It was super funny because when I was pitching the story to Studio Trigger, Roman wasn't in the story," Sztybor explained. "While working on the storyline and getting to know Kai Ikarashi better, we discovered that we are both cinephiles and love cinema. We had so many characters and realized we needed a POV character through whom we could see all the others—a connection between them. We thought, 'Okay, we love cinema; let me create a cinephile this season.' Going back to that constant dialogue between two seasons as a mirror: one of the themes of season one was losing innocence. We thought Roman could reference this theme by being a glimpse of innocence in a terrible city. That's why he loves retro things and is against braindances—he wants to maintain that innocence as long as he can." Roman isn't the only cinephile in Night City, as eagle-eyed fans can also spot Hideo Kojima making a cameo in the series. Cyberpunk: Edgerunners Season 2 consists of 10 episodes, and it'll be available starting October 20.

articles.title: Christiane Amanpour tore into CNN's new owner — and knew she had to quit
articles.description: When John Dickerson announced he was leaving CBS in October 2025, it was less than a month after David Ellison took control of Paramount, CBS’s parent, and appointed Bari Weiss to overhaul the news division. Weiss was, more or less, an opinion writer with no television news experience. Evening news anchor Dickerson, a CBS fixture for 16 years, said at the time he would be gone by year’s end. Everyone in the media business understood what it meant. The people who embodied the old CBS News were in danger of losing their jobs. Dickerson packed up before he would presumably be told to clean out his desk. Now it’s happening again, almost a year to the day. On Monday, Christiane Amanpour announced she is leaving CNN after 43 years, just weeks after Ellison’s Skydance closed its takeover of CNN’s parent company, Warner Bros. Discovery. Her statement said she was leaving after “many months of thought and a few sleepless nights.” CNN chairman Mark Thompson says they’ve discussed her exit for months. Nobody is saying it’s about Ellison. Of course they aren’t. Because it is, and anyone who thinks otherwise isn’t paying attention. As the old saying goes, fool me once, shame on you — if you thought Ellison would touch CBS. Fool me twice, shame on me — if you believe Ellison won’t touch CNN. Amanpour is not a nonpartisan bystander to the story, and she made her views known earlier this year about the new ownership. In May, she said she was concerned about CNN’s future “based on what’s happened to the other things” Ellison has taken over, “like CBS News.” Amanpour is the ShakeAlert before a severe earthquake arrives. It’s coming, and, like CBS News, it will be destructive for CNN. Ellison has promised CNN editorial independence. But he made promises about CBS, too. Reporting during the merger fight said he offered Trump administration officials assurances of sweeping change at CBS News, even as he told the public something else. CBS staffers felt betrayed. They were not only betrayed. They were slaughtered by a greedy, conservative billionaire who only cares about kowtowing to Donald Trump and couldn't care less about a free press. Look at how deplorable CBS became. Weiss has reportedly pushed CBS reporters to chase “thin theories” about Democratic Senate candidates. Semafor reports she directed “serious resources” toward linking Michigan’s Abdul El-Sayed to the Muslim Brotherhood and had staff pursue a rumor that Texas’s James Talarico was in a mental health facility. CBS staffers told reporters that her ideas routinely come from social media influencers and opposition research placed in conservative outlets. This is what “independence” looks like under Ellison. Is anyone else out there enraged about this reporting? Weiss is despicable, but I’m sure her boss, Ellison, is quite pleased. And I hate to be the bearer of bad news, but enjoy Ted Turner’s CNN for as long as you can, because it’s about to get torn apart, with money at the root, as usual. The combined company Ellison is running is carrying enormous debt, and Ellison has promised investors billions in annual savings. Every media merger in history ends the same way: the big salaries go. The new company ethos is cut, cut, cut. At CNN, that means the biggest names on the roster. Amanpour may simply be the sharpest tool in the shed. She’s reading the writing on the wall, leaving of her own accord, and implicitly warning that the knives are coming out. The next question is who becomes the next Bari Weiss, because the aforementioned Thompson, with four decades of broadcast experience, is surely on the chopping block. There’s no doubt in my mind. I’m speculating, but it’s informed speculation based on the CBS blueprint, that Ellison could install an outsider with no newsroom background and a mandate to disrupt and please the right-wing base. Imagine someone like Breaking Points’ Saagar Enjeti, a populist who built an audience by telling people the cable news establishment is rotten. Ellison could pitch that as a new type of “balance” in news presentation. But someone like Enjeti — and that person is coming — would be like a bulldozer and wrecking ball at CNN. CNN has spent years trying to showcase a range of voices, and it has not gone smoothly. Scott Jennings is not only a jerk, but he’s been a disaster — mmm, well, maybe not so much, because he sure lights up social media. He’s the network’s most polarizing panelist. Whether you find him entertaining or, like me, annoying, think about how he looks to a new owner who wants a more right-leaning product. If Ellison wants a face for the new CNN, I wouldn’t bet against someone like Jennings. Can you imagine? Well, yes, I can. If we base what will happen to CNN on what happened to CBS, then first comes the promise of independence. Then come the cost cuts — they will be far-reaching — followed by a new boss with a so-called “fresh perspective,” and then the numerous departures of the network’s most trusted voices. Dickerson was the first at CBS. Amanpour is the first at CNN. Amanpour’s parting advice to her colleagues was simple: “Always be truthful, not neutral.” CNN’s days of being neutral and truthful are numbered.
